title: Product Bazaar
tagline: Bonds, shares, funds, gold and REITs
principle: Product classes and what they mean
product: Government bonds, shares, mutual funds, index funds and ETFs, gold, REITs

lessons.title: Bonds: lending for interest
lessons.subtitle: Why bond prices fall when rates rise
lessons.capability: Explain what a bond is and why its price moves with interest rates.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: My uncle says bonds are 'boring'. What even is a bond?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: A bond is a loan you give, to the government or a company.
It pays you interest every year, called the coupon, and returns your money at the end.

steps.title: The rate seesaw
steps.caption: Drag the rate new bonds pay. Watch your old bond's price.

steps.question: Interest rates rise. What happens to the price of bonds you already own?

options.why: Right. New bonds pay more, so yours is worth less to a buyer.
That happens when rates fall.
Bond prices move with rates every day.

steps.question: When you buy a government bond, who is borrowing?

options.why: Yes. You lend; it pays interest and repays you.
You're the lender.
The bank might hold it for you, but the government borrows.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Government Bond
steps.realLife: Individuals can buy government securities through RBI Retail Direct. Held to the end, you get the interest and your money back; sold early, you get the market price.
steps.deeper: Yield to maturity is the return if you hold to the end. 'Duration' measures how much a bond's price moves when rates change: longer bonds move more.

lessons.title: Shares: owning a slice
lessons.subtitle: A piece of a real business
lessons.capability: Explain what owning a share means, and the risk of one company.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: I'm buying shares! Shares of what? Doesn't matter, the price will go up!

steps.speaker: kip
lines: A share is a slice of a real business. Over time, its value follows how that business does.

steps.title: Own a slice of Meena's Chai
steps.caption: Buy some shares, then try three different years.

options.text: You own a small part of the company
options.why: Right. Its profits and its losses are partly yours.
That's a bond.
Shares have no fixed return. That's the risk, and the reward.

steps.question: Why is putting everything in one company risky?

options.text: It can go bust, taking your money with it
options.why: Exactly. That's why investors spread out.
Some do, every year.
They can, on the stock exchange.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Shares
steps.realLife: Indian shares trade on the NSE and BSE through a demat account. A minor's demat account is opened and run by a parent or guardian.
steps.mission: Pick a company whose product you use. What does it sell, and does it make a profit?
steps.deeper: Earnings per share (EPS) is the profit for each share; the P/E ratio compares the share price to it. You'll use both in Analyst HQ.

lessons.title: Mutual funds: pooling
lessons.subtitle: Own 50 companies with ₹500
lessons.capability: Explain how a mutual fund pools money and spreads risk.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: What if you could own a little of 50 companies at once, with ₹500?
That's a mutual fund: many people pool their money, and a professional invests it.

steps.title: Basket builder
steps.caption: Pick a basket size. See what one bad year can do.

steps.question: Why does a fund with 50 companies lose less when one fails?

options.text: Each company is only a small slice
options.why: Right. One failure barely dents the basket.
They can. The whole market can fall.
No such guarantee for funds.
Yes: Net Asset Value, the value of everything the fund owns, per unit.
That's part of the fee, the expense ratio.
Funds don't guarantee returns.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Mutual Fund
steps.realLife: SEBI regulates mutual funds, and every fund publishes what it holds each month. You can start a SIP from about ₹100–₹500.
steps.deeper: 'Direct' plans skip the distributor's commission, so their yearly fee is lower than 'regular' plans of the same fund.

lessons.title: Index funds and ETFs
lessons.subtitle: The fee that compounds
lessons.capability: Compare index funds with active funds, and see how fees compound.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: My fund manager is a genius! He charges 2% a year, but it's worth it, right?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Maybe. But over the long run, most active funds don't beat their index after fees. And fees compound, just like returns.

steps.title: The fee that compounds
steps.caption: Drag the yearly fee. Watch 20 years of a ₹1,000-a-month SIP.

options.text: Copies a market index, like the Nifty 50, at low cost
options.why: Right. No stock picking, so fees stay tiny.

options.text: Lets a manager pick hot shares
options.why: That's an active fund.
Its value goes up and down with the market.

options.text: A fund that trades on the stock exchange like a share
options.why: Yes. Exchange-traded fund: bought and sold during market hours.
No, it holds shares, bonds or gold.
No, it's a regulated fund.

steps.title: In real life
steps.realLife: Nifty 50 index funds and ETFs often charge about 0.05–0.3% a year. ETFs need a demat account; index funds can be bought straight from the fund house.
steps.deeper: 'Tracking error' measures how closely a fund follows its index. The lower, the better.

lessons.title: Gold and commodities
lessons.subtitle: Shine, with no interest
lessons.capability: Explain what gold does in a portfolio, and the ways to own it.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Grandma says gold always goes up. So I'll put everything in gold!

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Gold often shines when people are scared or prices rise. But it pays no interest, and it has had long flat years.
A small slice can steady a portfolio.

items.title: Jewellery
items.text: Making charges and storage costs, and hard to sell at full value.

items.title: Coins and bars
items.text: Pure gold, but you have to store it safely.

items.title: Gold ETFs and funds
items.text: Track the gold price, with no storage worries.

items.title: Gold-linked government bonds
items.text: Follow the gold price and paid a little interest on top. Check whether new ones are on offer.

steps.title: Open your stall
steps.caption: Three customers. Recommend the right product.

steps.question: What is gold usually good for in a portfolio?

options.text: A steadying slice when fear or inflation rises
options.why: Right. A slice, not the whole thing.
Gold pays no income.
Gold has had long flat and falling years.

steps.title: Card unlocked: Gold
steps.realLife: Indian households hold a lot of gold, mostly as jewellery. Investors who want gold usually prefer ETFs or funds, which skip making charges and storage.
steps.deeper: Gold is priced in dollars globally, so in India its rupee price also moves when the rupee weakens or strengthens.

lessons.title: REITs: rent from big buildings
lessons.subtitle: Be a landlord with ₹500
lessons.capability: Explain what a REIT owns and how it pays you.

steps.speaker: dash
lines: Can I be a landlord with ₹500?

steps.speaker: kip
lines: Kind of! A REIT owns big rent-paying buildings, like offices and malls, and shares the rent with its unit holders.

items.title: What it owns
items.text: Offices, malls and warehouses that pay rent.

items.title: What you get
items.text: Most of the rent, paid out regularly.

items.title: The catch
items.text: Unit prices swing, and empty buildings mean less rent.

items.title: Its cousin, the InvIT
items.text: The same idea for roads and power lines.

steps.question: Where does a REIT's income mainly come from?

options.why: Right. Most of it is paid out to unit holders.
No, it's property income.
Unrelated.

steps.question: Why might a REIT's price fall?

options.text: Offices sit empty and rents drop
options.why: Yes. Less rent, less income, lower price.
It isn't.
They trade like shares and can fall.

steps.title: Card unlocked: REIT
steps.realLife: India has listed REITs that own office parks and malls. They trade on the stock exchange, and SEBI requires them to pay out most of their income.
steps.deeper: Small and medium REITs (SM REITs) are a newer SEBI category for smaller properties, with higher minimum investments.

lessons.title: Boss: Bazaar Bargain
lessons.subtitle: Everyone at your stall
lessons.capability: Match products to people's goals, time and risk.

steps.speaker: kip
lines: The final test of the Product Bazaar! Customers are queuing at your stall.
Match each one to the right product.

steps.brief: Market day! A Risk Lanes run: spread across SAFE, BALANCED and WILD, and keep cash for surprises.

steps.question: Someone wants steady income and can't afford losses. Best fit?

options.why: Right. Regular interest, very low risk.
Too risky for that goal.
No income, wild swings.

steps.question: The cheapest way to own the whole market?

options.why: Yes. Low fees, no stock picking.
That's a gamble, not the market.
Making charges, and it isn't the share market.

steps.title: World complete: Product Bazaar
steps.realLife: You now know what each product is, what it's for, and what it costs. They're all in your Practice Portfolio. Next, Portfolio Fort: combining them to survive market storms.
steps.deeper: Whatever the product, ask the same four things: what am I really owning, how could I lose money, how fast can I get it out, and what does it cost every year?
